newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian prosecutor to review MinFin freezes.
newsitem.headline: Russian prosecutor to review MinFin freezes.

text.p: Prosecutor-General Yuri Skuratov has ordered his staff to review all cases where MinFin bonds have been frozen by the authorities and if necessary to take measures to release them, Itar-Tass news agency said on Wednesday.
The review, which has already started, is to be completed within a month, it said, quoting a senior aide to Skuratov, Alexander Zvyagintsev.
Measures should be taken if necessary to release frozen bonds acquired in good faith, Tass said.
Skuratov said legal norms should be strictly observed when ordering the freeze of MinFin bonds held in depositaries.

Skuratov's order has been transmitted to the Interior Ministry, which is responsible for the police, the Federal Security Service, which handles domestic security and counter-espionage, the Federal Tax Police Service and the State Customs Committee, Tass said.
The government called on the judicial authorities at a meeting on November 5 to review cases of frozen MinFins.
Under criminal law police may freeze bonds which are said to be stolen, but under civil law bonds may not be seized from owners who acquired them in good faith.
The government has also asked the Interior Ministry and Prosecutor-General to submit proposals to the government on eliminating these legal contradictions by November 25.

A Moscow district prosecutor's office issued an order to freeze $56.81 million face value in June. The bonds were frozen as part of an investigation into the head of a small bank which has since closed.

This would bring the total bonds currently known to have been frozen to $74 million, including around $24 million already detailed by the finance ministry in July, some of which had been stolen in the breakaway republic of Chechnya.
Owners of previously frozen MinFins have not received coupon payments which the Finance Ministry transferred to Vneshekonombank, the paying agent.
Prices of the dollar-denominated MinFin bondss were hit during the summer when rumours that bonds had been frozen first began to circulate.
But prices have recovered in the run-up to the issue, likely later this month, of Russia's debut Eurobond.
The authorities are keen to resolve the frozen MinFin problem before the Eurobond issue.
